jurisdiction.name: United Kingdom
jurisdiction.overview: Nationally published records appear separately from applicable EU-level records. The landscape, historical relationships and legal applicability remain under document-level review.

narrative.summary: The United Kingdom has no AI-specific statute and regulates AI through existing law and sector regulators, following the principles-based approach set in the 2023 AI regulation white paper and the government's February 2024 response. The main binding rules are in data protection law, where the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 rewrote the rules on automated decision-making from February 2026 and requires an ICO code of practice on AI; in the Online Safety Act 2023 and the Crime and Policing Act 2026, which create offences around deepfakes and AI image generators; and in the Automated Vehicles Act 2024. Government policy is led by DSIT through the AI Opportunities Action Plan (2025), with the AI Security Institute testing frontier models and the Cabinet Office's AI Playbook and Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard governing public-sector use. Regulators including the ICO (now the Information Commission), CMA, FCA, Bank of England, Ofcom, MHRA and EHRC publish their own AI approaches, and the CMA has imposed a binding conduct requirement on Google's use of publisher content in generative AI. Scotland and Wales have their own AI strategies and Northern Ireland is consulting on its first.
lead_institutions: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
Information Commission (formerly the Information Commissioner's Office)
Financial Conduct Authority and Bank of England / PRA
Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency
Scottish Government, Welsh Government and Northern Ireland Executive
narrative.review_notes: A deep review completed on 7 October 2026 covered UK-wide legislation, central government, the main regulators, the Scottish, Welsh and Northern Ireland governments, and the Greater London Authority and other large cities; Jersey, Guernsey, the Isle of Man, Gibraltar and other Crown Dependencies and Overseas Territories are separate jurisdictions, and no AI documents from them came up. Ofcom, Equality and Human Rights Commission and Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum documents were checked against archived copies of their official pages, and several city council websites remain to be checked; pending are the ICO statutory code on AI and automated decision-making, Northern Ireland's final AI strategy, AI updates from other regulators such as Ofgem, Ofqual and the HSE, defence AI policy and AI policies of other councils.

instruments.official_title: Data Protection Act 2018
instruments.english_title: Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR (automated decision-making framework)
instruments.current_status: Royal Assent 23 May 2018; main provisions in force 25 May 2018 (SI 2018/625). Read with the UK GDPR (retained Regulation (EU) 2016/679). The original automated-decision rules (UK GDPR Art. 22, DPA 2018 ss.14, 49-50) were replaced by UK GDPR Arts. 22A-22D and DPA 2018 ss.50A-50D, inserted by Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.80, in force 5 February 2026 (SI 2026/82, reg. 2(j)); decisions taken before that date stay under the old rules (reg. 5). Intelligence-services ADM rules (ss.96-97) amended by the same section. Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 ss.118-119, in force 30 September 2026 (SI 2026/1015), abolished the office of Information Commissioner and transferred its functions to the Information Commission. In force as amended.
instruments.summary: The UK's general data protection framework: the Data Protection Act 2018 together with the UK GDPR governs processing of personal data, including for training and using AI systems, and is enforced by the Information Commission, which replaced the Information Commissioner on 30 September 2026. Since 5 February 2026 its automated decision-making rules are UK GDPR Arts. 22A-22D (general processing) and DPA 2018 ss.50A-50D (law enforcement): significant decisions based solely on automated processing are restricted only where they use special category data or rely on recognised legitimate interests, and controllers must provide safeguards letting people get information, make representations, obtain human intervention and contest the decision. Part 4 (ss.96-97) separately governs automated decisions by the intelligence services.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Horizontal data protection law that governs AI training and use of personal data and sets the UK rules on solely automated decision-making and profiling.

instruments.official_title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025
instruments.english_title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025
instruments.current_status: Royal Assent 19 June 2025; commenced in stages by regulations under s.142 (nine commencement SIs to September 2026). Copyright and AI duties ss.135-137 in force 20 August 2025 (SI 2025/904); s.80 automated decision-making in force 5 February 2026 (SI 2026/82, Commencement No. 6, with a saving for pre-commencement decisions); s.138 purported intimate image offences in force 6 February 2026 (SI 2026/31, Commencement No. 5); ss.118-119 replace the Information Commissioner with the Information Commission from 30 September 2026 (SI 2026/1015). No regulations under UK GDPR Art. 22D or DPA 2018 s.50D found on legislation.gov.uk as of 28 October 2026.
instruments.summary: Wide-ranging data reform Act that, in s.80 and Sch. 6, replaces UK GDPR Art. 22 and DPA 2018 ss.49-50 with new automated decision-making rules (Arts. 22A-22D, ss.50A-50D): 'meaningful human involvement' defines a solely automated decision, restrictions now apply mainly to decisions using special category data, and every significant automated decision needs safeguards (information, representations, human intervention, contest), with powers for the Secretary of State to set further rules by affirmative regulations. Sections 135-137 required the Government to publish a copyright and AI economic impact assessment and report within nine months (with a statutory definition of 'AI system'), and s.138 inserts ss.66E-66H into the Sexual Offences Act 2003, creating offences of creating, or requesting the creation of, a purported intimate image (deepfake) of an adult without consent. It also lets regulations require Information Commissioner codes of practice (new DPA 2018 ss.124A-124B).
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Primary legislation reforming UK rules on automated decision-making, mandating government work on copyright and AI, and criminalising the creation of sexually explicit deepfakes.

instruments.official_title: Online Safety Act 2023
instruments.english_title: Online Safety Act 2023
instruments.current_status: Royal Assent 26 October 2023; commenced in stages (Commencement No. 1-7 regulations to April 2026); ss.55 and 231 in force at Royal Assent; s.188 (intimate image offences, including computer-generated images) in force 31 January 2024 (SI 2024/31). SI 2025/1352 made the s.66B intimate image sharing offence a priority offence from 8 January 2026. Section 216A (power to extend the Act to illegal AI-generated content and AI services) inserted by Crime and Policing Act 2026 s.248 from 29 April 2026; no regulations under it found as of 28 October 2026 (a progress report is due by 31 December 2026 under that Act's s.249). In force as amended.
instruments.summary: Ofcom-enforced online safety regime imposing illegal-content and child-safety duties on user-to-user and search services. Content generated by bots or automated tools counts as user-generated content where the tool is not controlled by the provider (s.55(4)), bot-generated content can amount to illegal content (s.59(12), s.192(7)), and 'proactive technology' expressly includes AI and machine-learning tools (s.231(10)); s.188 created the Sexual Offences Act 2003 s.66B offence of sharing intimate images, which covers images made or altered by computer graphics. Since April 2026 s.216A lets the Secretary of State, by regulations, impose illegal-content, CSEA-reporting and fraudulent-advertising duties on providers of AI services that generate content and extend Ofcom's powers to them.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Main UK online safety statute; applies to AI-generated content on regulated services and now carries a specific power to regulate generative AI services.

instruments.official_title: Crime and Policing Act 2026
instruments.english_title: Crime and Policing Act 2026
instruments.current_status: Royal Assent 29 April 2026. Section 248 (new Online Safety Act s.216A) and s.249 in force at Royal Assent (s.255(2)(k)). Section 99 (purported intimate image generators) in force 29 June 2026 (SI 2026/689, Commencement No. 1). Sections 72-76 (CSA image-generators and CSA image guidance offences) not yet in force as of 28 October 2026 (England and Wales by Home Office regulations; Northern Ireland and Scotland by the devolved authorities under s.255(8) and (10)). Partly in force.
instruments.summary: Omnibus criminal justice Act with several AI-specific provisions. Sections 72-74 create offences (up to 5 years) of making, adapting, possessing or supplying a 'CSA image-generator' - any program, electronic information or service made or adapted to create child sexual abuse images - in each UK jurisdiction, with ss.75-76 covering possession of guidance on creating such images; s.99 inserts Sexual Offences Act 2003 ss.66I-66K, making it an offence (up to 3 years) to make, adapt, supply or offer a tool for creating purported intimate (deepfake) images, with a reasonable-steps defence. Section 248 gives the Secretary of State power to extend the Online Safety Act 2023 to illegal AI-generated content and AI services, and s.249 requires a progress report to Parliament by 31 December 2026 unless draft regulations are laid first.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Criminalises AI tools built to generate child sexual abuse images or non-consensual intimate deepfakes, and creates the power to regulate AI chatbots and generators under the Online Safety Act.

instruments.official_title: Automated Vehicles Act 2024
instruments.english_title: Automated Vehicles Act 2024
instruments.current_status: Royal Assent 20 May 2024; most of Part 1 (authorisation, self-driving test, statement of safety principles) not yet in force. Commencement: ss.55-56 and regulation-making powers in ss.78, 88-89 from 1 January 2026 (SI 2025/1339); Part 5 permits for automated passenger services (except s.84 civil sanctions) from 15 May 2026 (SI 2026/437); Part 4 marketing restrictions from 7 January 2027 (SI 2026/731). Partly in force.
instruments.scope: Great Britain (most provisions extend to England and Wales and Scotland)
instruments.summary: Framework law for self-driving vehicles in Great Britain: a vehicle may be authorised only if it meets a 'self-driving test' (it can travel autonomously, safely and legally), assessed against a statement of safety principles that must aim for safety at least equal to careful and competent human drivers and be approved by Parliament. It makes authorised self-driving entities and no-user-in-charge operators responsible for vehicle conduct, gives the user-in-charge immunity for the manner of driving, creates information duties, offences and sanctions, restricts marketing terms such as 'self-driving' to authorised vehicles (Part 4), and sets up a permit scheme for automated passenger services (Part 5).
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Sector-specific statute regulating the safety, authorisation, liability and marketing of AI-driven automated vehicles.

coverage_audit.no_material_found_note: UK-wide legislation, central government, regulators, the devolved governments and local government were searched, and on 2026-10-13 each national department's own AI documents were searched as well. No AI document was found from the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office, the Department for Work and Pensions, the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs or the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. Ofcom, Equality and Human Rights Commission and Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum documents were checked against archived copies of their official pages, some council websites remain to be checked, three central-government documents are known only from summaries, and NHS England's guidance on AI ambient scribing products is a lead to check later.
coverage_audit.technical_note:
Method note (original): Deep review completed on 7 October 2026, covering UK-wide legislation, central government (DSIT, the AI Security Institute, the Cabinet Office and Government Digital Service, NCSC and policy departments), the main regulators (ICO, CMA, FCA, Bank of England, Ofcom, MHRA, EHRC and the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum), the Scottish, Welsh and Northern Ireland governments, and the Greater London Authority and other large cities. The Ofcom, Equality and Human Rights Commission and Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum websites could not be read automatically, so their documents were checked against archived copies of the official pages; several city council websites could not be read either. Pending: the ICO statutory code on AI and automated decision-making, Northern Ireland's final AI strategy, AI updates from other regulators (such as Ofgem, Ofqual and the HSE), defence AI policy, and AI policies of other councils. Jersey, Guernsey, the Isle of Man, Gibraltar and other Crown Dependencies and Overseas Territories are separate jurisdictions; no AI documents from them came up in this review.

Coverage note (original): Technical review notes: Backfill run 2026-10-07 in five parts (UK-wide legislation; central government; regulators; devolved governments; local government). ofcom.org.uk, equalityhumanrights.com and drcf.org.uk returned bot challenges (403); six records (Ofcom 3, EHRC 2, DRCF 1) were verified from Internet Archive captures of the same official URLs and are marked link_status inaccessible. Three central-government records are primary_source_located (AI cyber security code implementation guide PDF, AISI misuse-safeguards principles, DHSC adult social care AI guidance: only summaries read). Council sites that blocked automated access: cardiff.gov.uk and cardiff.moderngov.co.uk, glasgow.gov.uk, Liverpool City Region Combined Authority, camden.gov.uk; the london.gov.uk taskforce page (report read from the official PDF). GMCA policy is sourced from GMCA's committee-document system on civico.net. legislation.gov.uk full-text search returned no AI hits in Acts of the Scottish Parliament, Senedd or NI Assembly; its index may not cover every recent instrument. Information Commissioner abolished and functions transferred to the Information Commission on 30 September 2026 (DUAA ss.118-119, SI 2026/1015 reg 2); earlier ICO documents keep the ICO as issuer. No part of this run was interrupted, so no record was written before a restart; the 14 pre-existing records were re-checked against their official pages by the central-government and regulators parts. Ministry catch-up 2026-10-13 (PROTOCOL §2 ministry rule, applied after this country's deep review; one agent, 30 minutes, national ministries' own AI documents only, nothing else re-reviewed): 13 record(s) added. Ministries: Department for Education (schools): Using AI in education leaders' support materials 2025 (recorded); Generative AI and data protection in schools 2024 (recorded); generative AI policy paper and product safety standards already held; Higher education / research: no DfE or DSIT ministry-level AI rules for universities found (Office for Students is a regulator, out of scope here); Department of Health and Social Care: government response to the RHC on AI as a medical device 2025 (recorded); Using AI in adult social care already held; NHS England ambient scribing guidance (lead, page not readable); Ministry of Justice: AI and Data Science Ethics Framework 2025 (recorded); AI action plan for justice already held (its one-year-on update of 24 September 2026 is already noted in that record's status); Judiciary: AI Judicial Guidance 31 October 2025 (recorded); earlier versions as lead; Crown Prosecution Service: 'How the CPS will use AI' (lead, no stated date); Ministry of Defence: Defence AI Strategy 2022, Ambitious safe responsible 2022, JSP 936 Part 1 2024 (all recorded); Defence AI Playbook, TF RAID, Defence Secretary letter, JCN 1/18 (leads); HM Treasury: nothing of its own (G7 CEG statement and AI Economics Institute as leads); HM Revenue & Customs: generative AI guidelines for software developers already held; nothing new; Home Office (police, security, immigration): facial recognition legal framework consultation 2025 (recorded); Immigration Enforcement live facial recognition policy 2025 (recorded); police AI factsheet, police facial recognition guide, facial age estimation guide (leads); Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office: nothing found (only development funding calls and research outputs; Bletchley Declaration already held); Department for Work and Pensions: nothing found; Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs: nothing found; Department for Transport: Transport AI Action Plan 2025 (recorded); automated vehicles regulations already held; Department for Energy Security and Net Zero: Vision for an AI-enabled clean energy system call for evidence 2026 (recorded); energy datasets for AI call for evidence (lead); Department for Business and Trade: nothing new (AI Sector Deal achievements page only); Department for Culture, Media and Sport: nothing new (copyright and AI documents already held); Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government: nothing found (digital planning tools guidance mentions AI only in passing); Intellectual Property Office: copyright and AI code-of-practice programme page (2023) not a code; nothing new; Cabinet Office / civil service: Ethics, Transparency and Accountability Framework for Automated Decision-Making 2021 (recorded; not previously held); other public-servant guidance already held. Not reached: none. Could not verify: NHS England 'Guidance on the use of AI-enabled ambient scribing products in health and care settings': england.nhs.uk returned HTTP 202 bot-check to curl; held as lead..
